\chapter{What the Air Carries}
\label{ch:ml-what-the-air-carries}
\hlchaptermodality{59}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name wind, sand, mud, smoke and an ember in Malayalam.}

Complete ML-C59-ember and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kāṟṟŭ]{\ml{കാറ്റ്} (kāṟṟŭ) — wind}

\label{lesson:ML-C59-wind}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{vēṇṭa} mean, and what did \emph{pōruṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കാറ്റ്}}
\textbf{\ml{കാറ്റ്}} (\emph{kāṟṟŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}wind\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{kāṟṟu}. The doubled \ml{റ്റ} in the middle is one of the harder things Malayalam asks of a new mouth: a trilled \emph{ṟ} held long, closer to a \emph{tt} made further back than to anything English has.

In Kerala the word is bound up with the monsoon, and the wind that brings it off the Arabian Sea has its own name in the local calendar. A fisherman's day is decided by \ml{കാറ്റ്} before it is decided by anything else.

It also does the work English gives to \emph{air}, so a room with no \ml{കാറ്റ്} is a stuffy room rather than a still one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things the weather brings.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kāṟṟŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pōruṁ}, then \emph{kāṟṟŭ}, and hold the doubled sound in the middle
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കാറ്റ്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}wind\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maṇal]{\ml{മണൽ} (maṇal) — sand}

\label{lesson:ML-C59-sand}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kāṟṟŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മണൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{മണൽ}} (\emph{maṇal}) — \textquotedblleft{}sand\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{maṇal}. The \ml{ണ} is retroflex, made with the tongue curled back, and the chillu \ml{ൽ} closes the word without a vowel after it — both of them sounds you have already been handling.

Kerala's sand is a river business as much as a beach one. Sand is dredged from the beds of the rivers that this book has already given you a word for, and the trade is argued about constantly.

The retroflex \emph{ṇ} is what separates this from a different word altogether, so the tongue position is carrying meaning rather than decorating it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the wind, and something it moves.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maṇal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kāṟṟŭ}, then \emph{maṇal}, and curl the tongue back for the middle of the second
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{മണൽ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sand\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ceḷi]{\ml{ചെളി} (ceḷi) — mud}

\label{lesson:ML-C59-mud}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maṇal} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ചെളി}}
\textbf{\ml{ചെളി}} (\emph{ceḷi}) — \textquotedblleft{}mud\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and it names wet mud — the kind a monsoon makes, not the dry earth underneath it.

Kerala spends several months a year in it, and the word carries a mild disgust that the English one does not quite have. To say a thing has \ml{ചെളി} on it is to say somebody should deal with that.

The \ml{ള} at the end is the retroflex \emph{ḷ}, tongue curled back again, and it is a different letter from the \ml{ൽ} that closed the sand-word. Malayalam distinguishes three \emph{l} sounds, and this run has now used two of them.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the monsoon is doing the work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ceḷi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{maṇal}, then \emph{ceḷi}, and hear the two different l-sounds at the end
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{ചെളി} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}mud\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puka]{\ml{പുക} (puka) — smoke}

\label{lesson:ML-C59-smoke}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ceḷi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{പുക}}
\textbf{\ml{പുക}} (\emph{puka}) — \textquotedblleft{}smoke\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{pukai}, and Malayalam has clipped the tail off where Tamil kept it — the same direction of travel you saw in the bone-word.

A Kerala kitchen fire makes a great deal of \ml{പുക}, and the word covers steam and vapour as well, so a hot vessel and a smouldering one can be described with it alike.

It is a short word doing a wide job, which is common in this layer of the language: the oldest words tend to be the briefest and the busiest.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one rises.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{puka}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ceḷi}, then \emph{puka}, and say which of the two you would see from a distance
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{പുക} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}smoke\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kanal]{\ml{കനൽ} (kanal) — an ember, a live coal}

\label{lesson:ML-C59-ember}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{puka} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കനൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{കനൽ}} (\emph{kanal}) — \textquotedblleft{}an ember, a live coal\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{kanal}, and it names the live coal rather than the flame — what is left glowing when a Kerala kitchen fire has burned down, and what is banked at night to be woken in the morning.

That is a distinction the language keeps carefully. The flame is one thing, the smoke you have just had is another, and the \ml{കനൽ} is the third: the part that holds the heat after the rest has gone.

The chillu \ml{ൽ} closes it, the same bare \emph{l} that closed the sand-word and the field-word before that.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: the wind, the sand, the mud, the smoke, and the ember that outlasts the fire.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kanal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{kāṟṟŭ}, \emph{maṇal}, \emph{ceḷi}, \emph{puka}, \emph{kanal}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കനൽ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}an ember, a live coal\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
